subject: economics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: An outward shift of the entire PPF is most likely caused by:
options: An increase in the quantity or quality of factors of production
A reallocation of resources between the two goods
A movement from inside to a point on the curve
questions.explain: Economic growth shifting the PPF outward requires more or better resources or improved technology.

questions.q: Moral hazard arises when:
options: A party changes its behaviour after a transaction because it no longer bears full risk
Buyers and sellers have identical information
questions.explain: Moral hazard occurs post-contract when one party takes greater risks because the costs fall on another party, a result of asymmetric information.

questions.q: A necessity good with few substitutes typically has demand that is:
questions.explain: Necessities with few substitutes have inelastic demand because consumers continue buying despite price changes.

questions.q: Making automatic pension enrolment the default option exploits which behavioural insight?
questions.explain: Default options exploit inertia, as people tend to stick with the pre-set choice rather than opt out.

questions.q: Which is a likely unintended consequence of a high tax on sugary drinks?
options: A complete end to all consumption
A guaranteed rise in producer profits
Substitution toward untaxed but equally unhealthy products, or smuggling
questions.explain: High indirect taxes can prompt substitution to untaxed alternatives or illicit markets, an unintended consequence reducing effectiveness.

questions.q: A good with a PED of -0.4 is described as:
questions.explain: A coefficient between 0 and -1 means demand is price inelastic, so quantity changes proportionately less than price.

questions.q: Non-rivalry in consumption means that:
options: One person's consumption reduces the amount available to others
One person's consumption does not diminish the amount available to others
People can be excluded from consuming the good
questions.explain: Non-rivalry means the good can be consumed by additional people at no extra cost and without reducing others' consumption.

questions.q: The 'tragedy of the commons' is most closely associated with:
options: Over-exploitation of a non-excludable but rival common resource
questions.explain: Common-access resources are rival but non-excludable, so individuals over-use them, depleting the resource for all.

questions.q: Government failure occurs when intervention:
options: Increases consumer surplus without any cost
Results in a net welfare loss or a misallocation of resources
questions.explain: Government failure arises when state intervention causes a more inefficient allocation of resources than would have existed otherwise.

questions.q: In the price mechanism, the rationing function refers to:
options: Prices incentivising producers to supply more
Prices rising to allocate scarce goods to those willing to pay
Prices signalling where resources should move
questions.explain: The rationing function uses rising prices to distribute scarce goods to consumers who value them most.

questions.q: A normal good that is a luxury has a YED that is:
questions.explain: Luxuries are income elastic with YED greater than one, so demand rises more than proportionately with income.

questions.q: A subsidy granted to producers of a good with positive externalities shifts the:
options: Supply curve to the left, raising price
Supply curve to the right, lowering price and increasing output toward the social optimum
questions.explain: A producer subsidy lowers costs, shifting supply right so output rises toward the optimum where MSB equals MSC.

questions.q: Regulatory capture is an example of government failure in which:
options: Regulators act in the public interest at all times
A regulator comes to serve the interests of the firms it is supposed to regulate
questions.explain: Regulatory capture occurs when the regulating body is dominated by the industry's interests rather than protecting consumers.

questions.q: A quasi-public good differs from a pure public good because it:
options: Has the potential to be made excludable or is partly rival
questions.explain: Quasi-public goods (e.g. a beach or a road) only partially satisfy non-rivalry and non-excludability and can sometimes be made excludable.

questions.q: Scarcity arises fundamentally because:
options: Wants are unlimited but resources are finite
questions.explain: The basic economic problem is that finite resources cannot satisfy unlimited human wants.

questions.q: A specific (per-unit) indirect tax shifts the supply curve:
options: Vertically upwards by a larger amount at higher prices
Vertically upwards by a constant amount
questions.explain: A specific tax adds a fixed amount per unit, shifting supply up by the same vertical distance at every quantity.

questions.q: A subsidy granted to producers will, ceteris paribus:
options: Shift the supply curve to the left and raise price
Shift the demand curve to the right
Shift the supply curve to the right and lower equilibrium price
questions.explain: A subsidy lowers production costs, shifting supply right, increasing quantity and lowering market price.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is best defined as:
options: The total cost of all alternatives forgone
The next best alternative forgone when a choice is made
The sunk cost of a previous decision
The money price paid for a good
questions.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the single next best alternative sacrificed, not the sum of all alternatives.

questions.q: Adverse selection in an insurance market is an example of:
options: A problem arising from asymmetric information before a transaction
questions.explain: Adverse selection occurs when one party hides information before a deal (e.g. high-risk individuals more likely to buy insurance), a consequence of information asymmetry.

questions.q: A pure public good is best defined as one that is:
options: Provided only by the government and free at the point of use
questions.explain: A pure public good is simultaneously non-rival (one person's use does not diminish another's) and non-excludable (people cannot be prevented from consuming it).

questions.q: 'Anchoring' as a behavioural bias means that consumers:
options: Rely too heavily on an initial reference value when making decisions
questions.explain: Anchoring describes over-reliance on a first piece of information, such as an original price, when judging value.

questions.q: Demand is said to be perfectly inelastic when the PED equals:
questions.explain: Perfectly inelastic demand has a PED of zero, shown by a vertical demand curve where quantity does not respond to price.

questions.q: A merit good is one that is:
options: Always provided by the free market efficiently
Over-consumed because consumers overestimate its private benefit
Under-consumed because consumers underestimate its private benefit and it has positive externalities
questions.explain: Merit goods are under-consumed because individuals undervalue the private benefit and external benefits are ignored, justifying intervention.

questions.q: Excludability means that:
options: The good has no external benefits
Consumption by one person reduces availability to others
It is possible to prevent non-payers from consuming the good
The good is provided by the state
questions.explain: Excludability refers to the ability to stop those who do not pay from consuming the good, a key feature distinguishing private from public goods.

questions.q: In behavioural economics, 'bounded rationality' refers to the idea that:
options: Decision-making is limited by information, time and cognitive capacity
questions.explain: Bounded rationality recognises that limited information and mental capacity prevent fully rational optimisation.

questions.q: Income elasticity of demand (YED) for an inferior good is:
questions.explain: An inferior good has a negative YED because demand falls as consumer income rises.

questions.q: A demerit good such as tobacco is characterised by:
options: Marginal private benefit exceeding marginal social benefit, causing over-consumption
Marginal social benefit exceeding marginal private benefit
questions.explain: Demerit goods are over-consumed because consumers overvalue the private benefit and ignore the external costs imposed on society.

questions.q: The deadweight welfare loss from a negative production externality is the area:
options: Above the supply curve at zero output
Between MSC and MPC, between the free-market and socially optimal outputs
questions.explain: The welfare loss triangle lies between the MSC and MPC curves over the range of over-production beyond the social optimum.

questions.q: A key limitation of using indirect taxes to correct externalities is that:
options: It is difficult to place an accurate monetary value on the external cost
questions.explain: Valuing externalities precisely is difficult, so the tax may be set too high or too low, risking government failure.

questions.q: Producer surplus is the area:
options: Below the supply curve and below price
Above the supply curve and below the market price
Below the demand curve and above price
questions.explain: Producer surplus is the difference between the price received and the minimum price firms would accept, shown above the supply curve.
